Atlantic bonito (Sarda sarda) is a fast-growing, highly migratory scombrid that attains a maximum recorded total length of 91.4 centimeters [Li = 91.4 centimeters], making it one of the smaller members of the tribe Sardini. Data collected from commercial catches in the Mediterranean and along the eastern Atlantic seaboard indicate that individuals typically reach this asymptotic size within five to six years, a growth trajectory that reflects the species' elevated metabolic demand and energetic investment in rapid somatic expansion. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this length has been estimated from length-weight regressions at approximately 9.7 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 9.7 kilograms], a mass that positions S. sarda as a medium-sized pelagic predator capable of exploiting a broad range of forage fish stocks. In contrast to its larger congener Sarda chiliensis, the Atlantic bonito achieves a considerably lower maximum body mass, consistent with its shorter lifespan and the cooler mean temperatures of its temperate-subtropical habitat.

Sexual maturation in Atlantic bonito occurs at a comparatively modest body size, with individuals reaching puberty at a total length of 37.8 centimeters [Lp = 37.8 centimeters]. This length threshold is reached relatively early in life, typically within the first two growing seasons, and is accompanied by a corresponding wet weight at puberty of roughly 585 grams [Wwp = roughly 585 grams]. The transition to reproductive maturity at such a moderate size is characteristic of an opportunistic life-history strategy, enabling individuals to contribute to the breeding population before mortality risks inherent to prolonged migration accumulate. Field studies using histological examination of gonadal tissue have confirmed that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis are initiated once individuals surpass this length, and that first spawning typically follows during the subsequent warm season.

Reproductive output in Atlantic bonito is substantial, reflecting a high-investment breeding strategy common among epipelagic scombrids. Under the thermal conditions typical of their spring and summer spawning grounds, measured at 10.7 °C [T = 10.7 °C], individual females have been observed to produce approximately 1223 oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1223 oocytes per spawning event] and engage in roughly 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly 365 spawning events per year], yielding a maximum daily reproduction rate that offsets high egg and larval mortality. This annual fecundity, based on the daily rate derived from the product of fecundity per event and event frequency, allows the species to maintain population stability despite substantial losses during the planktonic phase. The spawning period extends over several months in warmer regions, with gravid individuals exhibiting asynchronous oocyte development that ensures a protracted release of gametes into the water column.

The earliest life stages of Atlantic bonito are characterized by rapid development and minimal parental investment. Eggs are pelagic and transparent, with a diameter of approximately 1.05 millimeters based on measurements from the congener Scomber japonicus, and the resulting wet weight at birth has been calculated at 0.0006 grams [Wwb = 0.0006 grams]. At the typical incubation temperature of 10.7 °C [T = 10.7 °C], embryos complete development within about 3.5 days [ab = about 3.5 days], a brief embryonic period that is consistent with the high metabolic rates and fast life-history pace of scombrid fishes. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva is endotrophic for the first few days post-eclosion, relying entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. This rapid transition from lecithotrophy to active foraging is critical for survival in the oligotrophic pelagic environment.

The natural lifespan of Atlantic bonito is relatively short compared to many other pelagic teleosts, with field records and otolith-based aging studies indicating a maximum documented longevity of 5 years [am = 5 years] in wild populations at a temperature of 10.7 °C [T = 10.7 °C]. This abbreviated lifespan, set against the background temperature regime of 10.7 °C [T = 10.7 °C], imposes a narrow window for reproductive contribution and drives the species toward early maturation and high annual fecundity. Comparative analyses within the genus Sarda reveal that S. sarda exhibits the shortest maximum lifespan, consistent with its smaller asymptotic size and its occurrence in cooler, more productive temperate waters. Intraspecific variation in longevity has been noted across the species' range, with individuals from the warmer southern Mediterranean stock occasionally reaching six years, although such occurrences remain exceptional.
